notes.meaning: God tells the Israelites never to sacrifice an animal that is sick, injured, or defective. Offering a flawed animal shows contempt for God and is an abomination, which means something deeply offensive to Him. The Lord deserves our absolute best because He is holy, and pure sacrifices looked forward to the spotless offering of Christ.

Moses warns that if any man or woman in Israel is caught worshipping false gods, or bowing down to the sun, moon, or stars, they have broken God's covenant. A covenant is a sacred, binding agreement, like a marriage between God and His people. Turning to created things treated that holy relationship with treachery, no matter who committed the act.

Leaders could not act on mere rumors; they were required to investigate the matter thoroughly to make sure the report was true. If the terrible sin of idolatry was proven, the guilty person was brought outside the town gate and stoned to death. Carrying out the sentence at the gate publicly removed the sin and warned the entire community.

A person could be sentenced to death only if two or three witnesses testified to the crime. An execution could never take place based on the word of just one person. This strict rule protected innocent people from malicious lies, personal grudges, or honest mistakes.

The witnesses were required to throw the first stones, and then the rest of the community joined in. This heavy responsibility forced witnesses to be completely honest, since they had to carry out the sentence with their own hands. In this way, the whole nation worked together to remove evil and honor God.

When local judges faced a legal dispute that was too hard to solve, such as a difficult murder case or an injury lawsuit, they had to take it to the central sanctuary. There, the Levitical priests and the presiding judge would hear the facts and deliver an authoritative ruling. God provided this higher court to make sure justice was carried out fairly when local leaders were uncertain.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic commentary often identifies the presiding judge here as the high priest, who served as God's supreme representative with final authority over religious and civil matters alike.

notes.meaning: Once the higher court at the sanctuary announced its decision, everyone had to follow it exactly without straying to the right or to the left. The priests and judges were not inventing their own rules, but applying God's written law to the case. Submitting to their verdict put an end to endless fighting and preserved peace across the nation.

Anyone who proudly defied the final decision of the priest or judge was to be put to death. Open rebellion against God's appointed authorities threatened the foundation of the whole community and could not be tolerated. When the nation saw this severe penalty carried out, they would learn healthy respect for God's law and turn away from arrogance.

Moses foretells that when Israel settles in the land, the people will ask for an earthly king so they can be like the nations around them. God permitted this change, but the king had to be chosen by the Lord Himself and had to be a fellow Israelite, not a foreigner. A native ruler would protect the pure worship of God and serve as a living picture of the promised Messiah.

differ.view: Rulers are placed under God's law rather than above it, providing the foundation for constitutional government where the law governs the king.

notes.meaning: Israel's king was strictly forbidden to build up huge stables of horses or send people to Egypt to purchase them. Horses were the powerful weapons of the ancient world, and gathering them would tempt the king to trust in military power rather than in God. Returning to Egypt for trade or alliances would also endanger the people by drawing them back toward the idolatry and slavery from which the Lord had set them free.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic commentators interpret this verse as specifically forbidding military alliances with Egypt to secure cavalry, rather than an invasion or physical relocation.

notes.meaning: The king was also commanded not to take many wives or gather huge piles of gold and silver for himself. Surrounding rulers built large royal harems and stored vast treasures to show off their power, but multiple marriages would draw the king's heart away to false gods. Hoarding excessive wealth would burden the people with heavy taxes and lead to pride and selfish luxury.

When the king took the throne, he was required to write out his own personal copy of God's law using the standard scroll kept by the Levitical priests. He was to keep this copy close by and read from it every day for the rest of his life. Writing and reading Scripture daily trained the ruler to revere the Lord and carefully obey every one of His commands.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The ancient Greek translation of the phrase for 'a copy of this law' gave rise to the title Deuteronomy, which literally means 'second law' or repetition of the law.

notes.meaning: Studying God's word daily prevented the king from thinking he was better than his fellow citizens, reminding him that he too was a servant under God. By staying faithful to the commandments without turning aside, the king would avoid tyranny and ensure a long, peaceful dynasty for his family. True leadership remains humble before God and treats subjects like brothers.
